extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, fact-checkers, and public health communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Provide standards and examples for identifying, debunking, and avoiding misinformation about COVID-19 (false prevention/treatment claims, legal/ethical misstatements, and misleading public-health messaging). The page lists incorrect claims and authoritative corrections or guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonality claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that the warm weather of the spring will be the end of the Coronavirus, or that the virus cannot live in warm/tropical temperatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While flu is seasonal in some countries, whether COVID-19 will show seasonality has not yet been determined; COVID-19 spread along international air travel routes and did not bypass tropical locations, so avoid definitive seasonal-end assertions without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breastfeeding guidance during COVID-19
rubrics_metrics.description: WHO and UNICEF advise that women should continue to breastfeed during the COVID-19 pandemic even if they have confirmed or suspected COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence as of May 2020 indicates it is unlikely COVID-19 can be transmitted through breast milk. Public messaging should follow WHO/UNICEF guidance rather than commercial substitutes promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual transmission and infertility claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that COVID-19 is sexually transmitted or causes permanent infertility based on detection of virus in semen or small studies reporting sperm abnormalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SARS-CoV-2 can persist in semen but cannot replicate in the reproductive system; mechanisms (viral entry into testes vs fever-related heat effects) exist for temporary sperm changes. Avoid broad claims of sexual transmission or long-term infertility absent robust evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handwashing standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Washing in soap and water for at least 20 seconds is the best way to clean hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is recommended by the CDC as the best method in most situations. If soap and water are not available, use a hand sanitizer that is at least 60% alcohol unless hands are visibly dirty or greasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand sanitizer efficacy threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: A hand sanitizer should be at least 60% alcohol to be an effective alternative to soap and water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most commercially sold hand sanitizer inactivates SARS-CoV-2, but effectiveness depends on ingredients; sanitiser is recommended when soap and water aren't available, though it is not effective against all types of germs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain soap over antibacterial soap
rubrics_metrics.description: CDC and FDA recommend plain soap; there is no evidence that antibacterial soaps are better and limited evidence they might be worse long-term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health advice should not promote antibacterial soaps as superior for COVID-19 prevention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face-mask guidance must reflect evidence and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities initially made conflicting statements about public mask use; masks can limit spread and early dismissals in some countries were misleading or incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public messaging should reflect evolving evidence (masks can work), avoid misleading claims done to manage shortages, and be careful not to overgeneralize from limited studies (e.g., single-material neck gaiter studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid health-related mask myths
rubrics_metrics.description: False claims that masks cause low blood oxygen, high CO2, weakened immune systems, or antibiotic‑resistant pneumonia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims are not supported by evidence and should not be used to justify avoiding mask use when recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal exemption claims for mask mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) provides blanket exemption from mask requirements, or distribution of 'exemption' cards allegedly issued by government agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. DOJ has stated the ADA does not provide a blanket exemption. Cards claiming exemptions are fraudulent and not issued by government agencies; public information should not endorse such cards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcohol consumption is not protective
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to some reports, drinking alcohol does not protect against COVID-19 and can increase health risks; ingesting methanol/isopropanol is poisonous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public messaging must warn that drinking alcohol is not preventive and that consumption of non-beverage alcohols (e.g., hand sanitizer, methanol) can cause severe poisoning or death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tobacco and nicotine claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Early small observational studies led to claims that tobacco smoking might be preventative; later larger evidence shows smokers have increased chance of infection and more severe symptoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid promoting tobacco or nicotine as protective and follow larger, more reliable studies over preliminary surprising results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warm/hot drinks myth
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that drinking warm drinks (~30 °C / 86 °F) protects from COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WHO made no such recommendation; drinking hot water can damage oral mucosa. Do not attribute false recommendations to authoritative organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious-protection claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that religious faith or rites (Holy Communion, prayer gatherings, shrine visits) protect from COVID-19 and therefore do not require precautions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims are unsupported by evidence; continuing high‑risk practices led to outbreaks. Public-health guidance should not be supplanted by unverified religious immunity claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helicopter spraying/false-disinfectant claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that helicopters are or will spray 'COVID-19 disinfectant' over homes or communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No such spraying has taken place/been planned, and there is no agent suitable for such spraying; do not publicize or act on these rumors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food/folk remedy warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation of claims that specific foods (e.g., cabbage, Datura) or practices prevent COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims can be false and dangerous (e.g., Datura poisoning); avoid promoting unverified dietary or folk remedies and highlight documented harms when they occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitamin D evidence caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Some studies/meta-analyses show weak evidence that increased vitamin D may reduce ICU admission but no effect on mortality; viral preprints and fraudulent papers circulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on systematic reviews and high-quality evidence; be cautious about preprints and investigate author/institutional credibility before promoting findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vaccine misinformation and hesitancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfounded conspiracy theories and misrepresentations about COVID-19 vaccines (side effects, immune system mechanics, manufacturing) have proliferated and may increase vaccine aversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter misinformation with accurate scientific explanations, transparent information about vaccine safety and manufacturing, and avoid amplifying conspiratorial narratives that erode trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in claims about incentives and mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: Misinformation has arisen regarding the legality and effect of incentives, mandates, and policies used to increase vaccination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing incentives or mandates, distinguish legal arguments from policy and avoid false claims about their legality or efficacy; reference authoritative legal and public‑health sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading indicators of hospital burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Using superficially empty hospital parking lots or sparsely populated hospitals to claim the pandemic is exaggerated is misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hospitalized case counts, ICU occupancy, and aggregate data are more reliable indicators than isolated videos or images shared to suggest hospitals are empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Untested and unproven treatments should not be promoted
rubrics_metrics.description: Widely circulated posts promoted unfounded treatments; some promoted methods are scams or dangerous (e.g., ingesting disinfectants, cow dung/urine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not promote treatments without clinical evidence; heed regulatory bodies (FDA/WHO/EMA/IDSA) advising against use (e.g., ivermectin for COVID-19). Highlight harms and legal consequences of promoting fraudulent cures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory-approval and endorsement accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a drug was approved by the WHO (e.g., 2-DG) or that a treatment 'helped' many patients without proper evidence are misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press statements and reports must accurately report which agencies have approved/endorsed a treatment and on what evidence; beware and correct false attributions of WHO or other agency approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangerous substances and fraudulent remedies (MMS, colloidal silver)
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotion of Miracle Mineral Supplement (chlorine dioxide) or colloidal silver as remedies has been fraudulent and dangerous, prompting regulatory action and legal penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and call out known fraudulent/dangerous products; regulators' cease-and-desist orders and prosecutions are indicators of illegitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate traditional medicine claims critically
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale promotion or mandatory use of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) in some official guidelines occurred despite lack of standard clinical evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat traditional-medicine claims as you would any therapeutic claim — require clinical evidence of safety and efficacy before endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize small, preliminary, and fraudulent studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints and small studies can go viral despite being flawed or fraudulent (e.g., fabricated affiliations); mainstream media and even some authoritative bodies have at times amplified such work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify study provenance, sample size, peer review status, and author/institution credibility before using results to inform public claims; meta-analyses and reputable agencies are more reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent-carrier claims rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that anyone infected will have the virus in their bodies for life are false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most infected people recover and eliminate the virus; messaging should avoid suggesting universal permanent infection while acknowledging long COVID and ongoing risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of denialist and conspiratorial framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that the pandemic is faked, exaggerated, or mischaracterized are characterized as pseudoscience and may lead to broader conspiratorial ideologies and hate (e.g., antisemitism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter denialism with evidence, and be aware that conspiracy theories can act as gateways to extremist or hateful narratives; avoid amplifying such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing: avoid using past tense prematurely
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the past tense to describe COVID-19 ('the pandemic is over') can misrepresent ongoing harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WHO leaders advise against past-tense framing while the virus continues to cause acute disease, long COVID, and excess deaths; maintain accuracy about the current state of spread and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combat the 'infodemic' by relying on trustworthy sources
rubrics_metrics.description: WHO described a 'massive infodemic'—an over-abundance of false information making it hard to find trustworthy guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer authoritative sources (WHO, CDC, peer‑reviewed research), fact-check claims, and avoid amplifying unverified social-media content; efforts to combat misinformation should prioritize clarity and trust-building.
